To use lo + adjective as a noun: lo bueno, lo malo, lo mejor, lo peor, lo importante.
To use lo que = what (the thing that): Lo que necesito es dormir.
To use lo + adjective/adverb + que for intensity: lo cansada que estoy, lo bien que habla.
To use lo de for “the thing about…”.
To review the unit: en caso de que, a menos que, ya que, para que, por mucho que.
Mid-October. In two days, Ana, Mihai, Rosa Elena and Elena fly to Kyoto for Yuki’s wedding. In the living room there are four open suitcases and clothes everywhere.
Ana, you don’t know how hard it is to fit all this into one suitcase.
I know perfectly well. I’ve been struggling with Rosa Elena’s for two hours. The bad thing about travelling with a small child is that she needs more things than the two of us put together.
Well, the good thing is we don’t have to carry food. There’s everything in Japan.
Tell your mother that. She’s prepared three jars of zacuscă for Yuki “in case she doesn’t like Japanese food”.
(laughs) Yuki is Japanese, Mum. The thing is, my mother doesn’t trust anything she hasn’t cooked herself.
Hey, and the kimono business? Did Takeshi answer you?
Yes. He says his family will lend each of us one, since it’s a traditional wedding. But we have to go a day early so they can fit them on us.
How exciting! What I want most is to see Yuki dressed as a bride at the shrine.
What worries me is the flight. Fourteen hours with a girl who’s nearly four…
However much she cries, people will understand. And besides, she has her granny. You don’t know how well she behaves with Elena.
That’s true. Well, the important thing is that we’re all going together. The rest doesn’t matter.
Exactly. And now, will you help me with this suitcase? Unless you’d rather carry Rosa Elena’s clothes in your rucksack.

The first thing you need to know is that in Japan people don’t tip. What for us is a kind gesture can be almost an insult for them.
The best way to get around is by train. You can’t imagine how punctual they are: if a train is a minute late, the company apologises.

The flight left Bucharest at six in the morning, so by three they were all awake. Well, all except Rosa Elena, who was sleeping in her granny’s arms as if the world didn’t exist.

Elena had a huge bag that she refused to check in. Inside, wrapped in three layers of newspaper, were the three jars of zacuscă, a jar of honey from her village and a hand-embroidered tablecloth she had made for the couple.
“Mum, they won’t let you through security with the jars,” said Mihai.
“We’ll see,” Elena answered, with the confidence of a woman who had spent forty years negotiating with officials.

The incredible thing is that she was right. At the security check, the officer took out one of the jars and looked at it suspiciously. Elena explained to him, in Romanian, what it was, who it was for and how important that wedding was. She told him about Yuki, about the shrine in Kyoto, about the kimono. The officer, a young man who probably had a similar grandmother, ended up smiling and handed the jar back.
“Have a good trip, madam,” he said. “And congratulations to the bride and groom.”
Mihai couldn’t believe it. Ana was laughing so hard she had to lean against the wall.

They had a stopover in Istanbul. The bad thing was that the first flight arrived late and they had to run through the whole airport with the little girl, the rucksacks and Elena’s famous bag. The good thing was that, with all the running, Rosa Elena laughed the whole way, convinced it was a game.
They reached the boarding gate just as it was closing. The flight attendant, seeing the granny panting with her bag, opened it again and let them through.

The second flight, the long one, lasted eleven hours. Mihai had read every possible tip online for travelling with small children: bring new toys, give her something to eat at take-off so her ears don’t hurt, walk up and down the aisle every hour. What no blog said was what to do when the child decides not to sleep.

Rosa Elena decided not to sleep. For the first four hours, however hard her parents tried, the little girl didn’t close her eyes. She wanted to see the clouds. She wanted to touch the screen. She wanted to say hello to all the passengers. Above all, she wanted to walk up and down the aisle, and there was no persuading her otherwise.

Then something unexpected happened. In the row in front sat an elderly Japanese lady, very elegant, with white hair in a bun. She turned round, looked at Rosa Elena and said something to her in Japanese in a very gentle voice.

The little girl went still, fascinated. The lady took a sheet of coloured paper out of her bag and, with very nimble fingers, folded a paper crane. She gave it to Rosa Elena. Then she made another, and another, and another.
Ana, who had learned a little Japanese with Yuki, managed to thank her: “Arigatō gozaimasu”. The lady smiled and answered in perfect English.
Her name was Mrs Tanaka. She was going back to Japan after visiting her son, who worked in Vienna. When Ana told her they were going to a wedding at the Shimogamo shrine, the lady’s eyes widened.
“I got married there,” she said. “Fifty-two years ago. What I remember best is the sound of footsteps on the gravel and how quiet the forest was. You’ll see. It’s the most beautiful thing there is.”

They talked for hours. Mrs Tanaka explained what they had to do during the ceremony: when to bow, when to clap twice, why the bride wears a big white hood that covers almost her whole face. Elena listened closely and every now and then asked something, which Ana translated.
Meanwhile, surrounded by paper cranes, Rosa Elena had finally fallen asleep, with a red crane in her hand.

When the plane landed in Osaka, it was night again. The strange thing about jet lag is that you don’t know if you’re tired or awake, if it’s today or tomorrow. Mihai looked at his watch and couldn’t work out how many hours they had been travelling.
At the exit, Mrs Tanaka said goodbye to them with a deep bow. Before leaving, she gave Ana a small envelope.
“For the bride and groom,” she said. “In case they don’t have enough cranes.”

Inside were a thousand tiny paper cranes, strung together on a golden thread. Ana recognised it: it was a senbazuru, the traditional gift that, according to legend, brings a thousand years of happiness. Mrs Tanaka must have made them during the flight without them noticing, or perhaps she was taking them for someone else and had decided to give them to them.
When Ana looked up to thank her, the lady had already disappeared into the crowd.

On the train to Kyoto, Rosa Elena was asleep again, now in her father’s arms. Elena was looking out of the window at the lights of the towns, without saying anything. Ana held the envelope of cranes in her lap, with both hands on top, as if it were a treasure.
“Do you know what the best thing about the trip was?” Mihai asked her in a whisper.
“No. The thing with my mother at the security check. I’ll never forget that as long as I live.”
Elena, who was pretending not to listen, smiled at the window. In her bag, wrapped in newspaper, the three jars of zacuscă were heading for Kyoto safe and sound.

It was nearly eleven at night when they reached Kyoto station. On the platform, among the people getting off the train, they saw two figures waving their arms with all their might. It was Yuki and Takeshi. Yuki was holding a handmade sign, with crooked letters, in three languages: «Bienvenidos», “Bine ați venit” and «ようこそ».

Ana dropped her bag and ran to her. She hadn’t known how much she had missed her until that moment. They hugged in the middle of the platform, laughing and crying at the same time, while the Japanese passengers walked round them in silence, discreetly, as if it were the most normal thing in the world.
“You came,” Yuki kept saying. “I can’t believe it. You came.”
And Takeshi, with a very serious bow, took Elena’s bag. It was so heavy he nearly fell over, and Elena, for the first time on the whole trip, burst out laughing.

That night, in the little guesthouse Yuki had booked for them by the Kamo river, nobody managed to sleep. The strange thing about jet lag, once again. Ana and Mihai sat on the tatami floor by the open window and listened to the sound of the water.
Ana opened Mrs Tanaka’s envelope and carefully took out the senbazuru. The thousand cranes glittered in the moonlight: red, blue, gold, white.

“Do you realise how strange it all is?” she whispered. “Five years ago I didn’t even know Kyoto existed. And now I’m here, with my daughter, with your mother, with a present from a stranger, at the wedding of a student who has become my sister.”
Mihai didn’t answer. He put an arm around her shoulders and they stayed like that until the sky behind the mountains began to turn pink.
